# 16-pairio — sources

Back-test entry `16-pairio.yaml`: Pairio, a voice assistant that helps factory technicians fix broken machines (YC
Spring 2026, P26). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named
(the launch-era site is in German; its quotes are given in German, with the author's English in brackets). "Author's
choice" marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent. The launch era is the Launch YC
post of 2026-04-21 and the weeks around it (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era where one
exists; anything later is marked as later).

Main sources (short names used below):
- [LYC] Launch YC: "Pairio – Fix broken equipment in factories faster", 2026-04-21 (created_at in the page data) — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Q18-pairio-fix-broken-equipment-in-factories-faster

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Maintenance technicians and operators who fix machines on the production line.
   [LYC] "Pairio helps technicians and operators resolve faults faster with voice AI." [YCP] "AI mobile app that helps
   factory technicians fix broken machines". → `roles[technician]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`. Author's choice: the
   technician only (operators are named too, but the fix and the report are the technician's).

2. **What (the job).** Get the machine running again fast, and keep the fix for the next person.
   [LYC] "Unplanned equipment downtime costs global industries over $1.4 trillion every year – and the root cause isn't
   broken machines. It's broken knowledge transfer." [LYC] "With the average technician in the US now 50 years old,
   knowledge is literally walking out the door". → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At the machine, when it fails, and afterwards when the fix should be written down.
   [LYC] "When a machine fails, resolution speed depends almost entirely on whether the one guy who's seen this before is
   working that day"; "Valuable technical clues are buried somewhere across 400 pages of OEM manuals or locked in outdated
   software"; "After spending 6 hours getting the line back up, the last thing a technician does is sit down and write a
   detailed fault report to institutionalize their knowledge". [FAQ] "Fundamentals and practical ways to use Pairio in
   day-to-day maintenance work." → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: machine breakdown`. Author's choice: the window
   {5, WORKING_DAYS} (a working-day rhythm) and Frequency 2 to 4 working days out of 5 -- daily for the team, not for
   each technician (header); Prevalence `p_80_100`.

4. **Which people.** Technicians at US plants that keep their own maintenance team.
   [LYC] "Ask: Can you introduce us to plant and maintenance managers at US manufacturing firms?" [WB] "Pairio richtet sich
   an Unternehmen mit eigener Instandhaltung - vom Mittelstand bis zum Konzern." [Pairio is for companies with their own
   maintenance, from mid-sized firms to groups.] → `context.segment`, `market: US`; the German plants are in the header.

5. **Who pays.** The plant; the maintenance manager chooses, the plant manager agrees.
   [LYC] "If you know anyone in plant operations or maintenance in US manufacturing we'd love to talk with them". [WB]
   quotes a "Meister & Abteilungsleiter Instandhaltung" [foreman and head of maintenance] as a user. → `persona.
   decision_maker: {role: manager}`; Buyer and payer tests "The plant manager" (listed with "The IT department"):
   author's choice, no source names who signs. Purchase friction's tested item, "Connecting it to SAP or Maximo": [FAQ]
   "including systems such as SAP, IFS, IBM Maximo, Oracle EAM Cloud, Hexagon, SharePoint, Outlook, and Asset API"; [WB]
   "Die genaue Anbindung hängt von Ihrer IT-Landschaft ab." [The exact connection depends on your IT landscape.] The IT
   security review and the plant-wide rollout sign-off are the author's. Commitment's step, "run a pilot on one
   production line": [REF] "A clearly scoped pilot creates evidence"; "Following a two-month pilot, the solution was
   integrated in four weeks." (later than launch; the launch-era site offers "Kostenlose Demo" [free demo]).

6. **Mechanism.** Ask by voice or photo; answers from the manuals and past repairs; speak the fix, get a report.
   [LYC] "Simply ask and instantly receive any available technical clue"; "Speak and let Pairio structure their learnings
   into reusable know-how"; "Use photos and videos to capture even more contextual knowledge". [WB] "Sprache, Foto oder
   Video rein - fertiger Bericht raus" [voice, photo or video in, finished report out]; "Pairio erkennt Fehlerbild,
   Maßnahmen, Ersatzteile und erstellt einen strukturierten Bericht." [Pairio recognises the fault, the actions, the spare
   parts and writes a structured report.] [YCP] "Users just take a picture of the broken machine and we search thousands
   of pages of manuals to find the right solution." → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`; Compatibility (a phone
   allowed at the machine — tested; manuals as files; quiet enough to speak) and Adoption friction (speak the fix when
   done — tested; photograph the fault first) are the author's, from the mechanism's own needs and [BLOG] ("tools that fit
   how technicians actually work, on mobile, in loud environments"). Relative advantage: shorter_time from [WB] "-25%
   MTTR", less_help_needed from [LYC]'s "the one guy who's seen this before"; the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** No price public; the cost is technician time.
   [WB] "Kostenlose Demo" and "Demo buchen" [free demo; book a demo], no price; [SITE] "Book a free demo", no price.
   → `commercial.price` AMOUNT_PERIOD $600 to $1,200 per technician a year is **the operator's reading** (about $50 to
   $100 a seat a month; header). Existing sacrifice, HOURS 150 to 300 of the breakdowns per technician a year: author's
   arithmetic -- 3 to 6 hours a week of a technician's time lost to hunting through manuals, waiting for the one person
   who knows, extra trips for tools and parts, and the report written afterwards, over about 50 working weeks; the scale
   is set by [LYC]'s "6 hours getting the line back up" and by [WB]'s "-25% MTTR" and "-80% Ablageaufwand" (the shares
   the company says it removes). The rate, $31 an hour, is [BLS] "$30.82 per hour" (May 2025 median), the author's
   stand-in. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (hours never compare with dollars).

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from these public accounts; no respondent is a real person.
   [BLOG] "At a specialty manufacturer in Illinois, the maintenance team told me some shifts run with a single
   technician."; "The troubleshooting descriptions? Consistently useless. 'Reset machine.' 'Machine broken, fixed it.'
   'Called supplier.'"; "The work order says there's a problem with the injection molding machine. That's it. They show
   up, assess, go back for parts, come back again."; "When a conveyor goes down, every minute counts in a way that's
   directly visible to the customer."; "she'd watched a technician try to use ChatGPT out of desperation to solve a
   machine-specific problem."

## Status today

Same idea. [SITE] (English, 2026-10-22) describes the same assistant (fault reports, manual search, data analysis, work
instructions) now aimed at US plants, with the Knipping reference: [REF] "Knipping reduced mean time to repair (MTTR) by
25%, generated €500K in savings through avoided downtime, and achieved a 95% adoption rate." and "Four German locations
are already onboarded." [FAQ] "In suitable use cases, MTTR can be reduced by up to 25%, filing effort by up to 80%, and
onboarding time by up to 90%." Price today: still not public ("Book a free demo").

## Could not be sourced

- **Any price.** Nothing public at launch or today; the founder's price is the operator's reading (header, item 7), so the
  Price line measures that reading, not the company's price.
- **A per-plant money cost.** Only the global $1.4 trillion is public; the chain cost is the technicians' time instead
  (header).
- **The hours per technician a year.** The sources give one example (6 hours on one breakdown) and shares removed; the
  150 to 300 is the author's arithmetic.
- **A technician's hour.** [BLS]'s median stands in.
- **Who signs, and the purchase steps.** No source names the buyer above the maintenance manager; the plant manager, the
  IT department, the security review and the rollout sign-off are the author's (the SAP or Maximo connection is sourced).
- **How often one technician meets a breakdown.** "Day-to-day" is the team's rhythm; the 2 to 4 working days out of 5 is
  the author's.
- **First-person technician accounts.** No Launch HN or forum thread; the occasions are scripted from [BLOG] (the
  founder's own account of US visits) and [WB]'s two user quotes ("Mit der App kann ich alles direkt dokumentieren und
  muss mir keine Sorgen machen, dass ich etwas vergesse." [With the app I can document everything straight away and
  needn't worry about forgetting something.]).

founder.order_why: The recency screen (4) sits between two screens that both ask to define where the idea applies (3 and 5), so the context step is split around it instead of finishing before the time window is set.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 show the same kicker and question ('Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies'), so the context step reads as asked twice.
founder.missing: The second half of the job, writing down the fix after the line is back up, is never asked as its own belief: screens 8 and 9 test only the missing expert. The flow also has no screen for what Pairio does (ask by voice or photo and get answers from the manuals and past repairs, speak the fix and get a report), and none for who pays and at what price (the maintenance manager choosing, the plant paying per technician).

PRIMARY.order_why: It runs the way I'd tell it: confirm where I work, whether something went down this week, how often, what I'd want easier, then the last breakdown itself. The only snag is the first two screens both say 1 of 4.
PRIMARY.asked_twice: Screens 2 and 3 overlap: 'did a machine go down' and then 'on how many days', where the second already covers the first.
PRIMARY.missing: Nothing about how long the line was down, what the fix actually was, or how I wrote it up afterward, like whether 'Reset machine.' in the log was all that got recorded. Screen 5 also lumps asking the guy who's seen it before together with digging through the OEM manual, when those are two very different trips.

screens.why2: 'Found the fix', 'hunting for the fix' and 'most of the shift' are how my technicians talk about a breakdown.
screens.why3: Every technician knows how long they spent on their last breakdown before they found what was wrong.
screens.why4: The rungs are distinct and ordered, but all five are about finding the fix; none covers the other half of my job, leaving a record, so a tech who found it fast but logged only 'reset machine' has no row that fits.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my 'the one guy who's seen this before' and the 400 pages of OEM manuals, but the recorded bar points to 'Found it, logged a line or two', a row that is not on this list, so the bar has drifted from the rows shown.
screens.instead: Rows: Found the fix fast and wrote it up / Found it fast, logged a line or two / Spent a long time hunting for the fix / Spent most of the shift hunting / Never found the fix myself; with the bar fixed to 'below Found it fast, logged a line or two', matching a row on the list.

screens.why1: Picking who asks my technicians the questions is the natural last step before the link goes out, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: The choice is plain, but the hint mixes voice and video and the line that Keel records the voice I pick once for 400 credits needs a second read to work out what I am paying for.
screens.why3: As the founder I can judge which voice my technicians on a US plant floor would listen to, after hearing the two 5-second samples.
screens.why4: Two named interviewers, each with a sample to hear and a default already picked, is a complete choice, and the hint says people can still read and tap instead of talking.
screens.why5: The screen changes nothing I typed about the technicians, the breakdowns or the record of the fix, and it shows nothing of Pairio to the people who answer.
screens.instead: Who should ask your questions? Daphne (picked for you) or Saskia. Tap to hear each. Every question is also written on screen, so people can read it and tap or type instead of talking. The voice you pick costs 400 credits, once for this project.

screens.why1: Choosing how technicians answer belongs right before sending, after I have picked who asks the questions.
screens.why2: Mostly plain, but the doubled "Daphne Daphne" and the status "Still recording · ready in a few minutes" need a second read: is it the video still being recorded, or my study?
screens.why3: I know my technicians answer on a phone, often on a loud floor and sometimes where phones are restricted, so I can pick from what I know of them.
screens.why4: The three choices are complete and distinct, and the loud-room figure helps me judge Daphne, but the Daphne option's status line and the doubled name read oddly next to the clean "Read and tap · Ready now".
screens.why5: It names my maintenance technicians as typed and leaks nothing of Pairio to them; reading and tapping, with speech allowed in boxes, suits a noisy line.
screens.instead: How should maintenance technicians answer? — AI interviewer (Daphne asks aloud; they talk, type or tap; works on loud floors more than 9 in 10 times) · ready in a few minutes / Read and tap (speak or type in boxes) · ready now / Let them choose · ready when Daphne is

screens.why1: Once the questions and the answer mode are set, the last step is deciding who receives the interview, so this belongs at the end of the flow.
screens.why2: The choices are clear, but each label runs into its description with no break ('People I know by name I send each one…'), and 'the Contacts page' assumes I know a Keel screen I haven't seen, so it takes a second read.
screens.why3: I know how I reach technicians: the few plant people I know by name in the US, and the maintenance managers I'm asking to be introduced to.
screens.why4: My real route to US technicians is a maintenance manager passing the link to their crew, and that doesn't fit cleanly here; the open-link option comes closest but needs a Google sign-in many floor technicians won't have on a plant phone.
screens.why5: This only asks how I distribute the study, and nothing of Pairio or its roles leaks to respondents.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? — People I know by name (one link each) / A manager or contact passes it to their team (one link each, sent through them) / People found with Keel's contact search / One open link posted where technicians already are

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits under the title with 'Frequency: 4 answered' beside it, but the '5 needed' that decides it is only down on the card, and nothing says why Frequency is named when Importance and Current solution are short by the same count, or why only 4 of the 7 who answered (6 of whom had a breakdown) were asked.
screens.why_b2: There is no chart; the tally '1 holding · 3 too few · 7 people answered' mixes cards and people, so it takes a second look to see it is 1 of 4 beliefs holding, while each card's bar ('bar 6 of 7', '5 needed') is plain.
screens.why_b3: The four names and belief lines are the ones I checked word for word (Importance's two-of-five, Current solution's 'asking whoever has seen the fault or digging through OEM manuals'), and the statement is my Launch YC problem with the $1.4 trillion softened to 'an enormous sum'.
screens.why_b4: The only hint of a next step is '5 needed to call it' on each card; the page never says to get one more technician who had a breakdown through the rest of the study before I read Importance or Current solution, which are the beliefs I care about.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, Prevalence is marked 'at the bar' rather than strong, and the three short cards are called too few instead of being given a lean.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 3 of the 4 beliefs had only 4 answers and need 5, because only the 6 technicians who had a breakdown were asked and 2 of those didn't finish. Get at least 1 more technician with a breakdown in the last 5 working days through the study before you read Importance or Current solution. Prevalence holds, but only just, at 6 of 7.

screens.why_b1: 'Holding up' sits right beside '6 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7 · at the bar', so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows 6 for and 1 against over 7 people on a 0 to 7 axis, with my bar marked at 6 and labelled 'at least 8 in 10', so I get it on first look.
screens.why_b3: It is my belief in my words: at least 8 in 10 technicians had a machine go down on their line in the last 5 working days, matching the actor, window and threshold I set.
screens.why_b4: The So line confirms breakdowns are common and points me to Frequency and Importance, but it doesn't say what this means for Pairio, such as that the moment the app is built for shows up nearly every week.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, 'a small group: a lean, not a call' is stated, and 'Holding up' is not overstated, though it could add that one more 'no' would drop it below my bar.
screens.instead: 6 of 7 had a machine go down this week, exactly at your bar: one more 'no' and it falls short. The breakdown moment Pairio is built for is real for nearly all of them, so next see how often it happens and whether fixing it fast is what they want help with.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Too few to call' sits right beside '4 answered · 5 needed to call it', and the So line repeats '4 counted, 5 needed', so I know why there is no call.
screens.why_b2: Working days out of 5 and the median at 1 day read at once, but the legend 'what you said at what you said beyond, the good side short of it' is garbled, and 'your bar · 3 of 4' next to a strip with one ghost cell takes a second look to see what the bar asks of whom.
screens.why_b3: 'Machine on their line go down on 2 to 4 working days out of 5' is my own Frequency line from the header, in my words.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it doesn't tell me to get one more counted technician, and it doesn't say the early lean is against me (3 of 4 below, middle answer 1 day), which would make me ask whether breakdowns hit each technician less often than the team's daily rhythm.
screens.why_b5: 'A lean, not a call' is honest, but the verdict's '4 answered' clashes with the count line's '6 answered · 4 counted', which blurs who actually replied.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 4 of 6 counted, 5 needed. So far it leans against you, with 3 of 4 seeing a breakdown on fewer days (middle answer 1 day), so get one more counted technician and check whether breakdowns are daily for the team but not for each technician.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '4 answered · 5 needed to call it', and the So line repeats '4 counted, 5 needed', so I know it's unsettled and why.
screens.why_b2: The bars count 8 picks from 4 people and the bar reads '3 of 4', but the strip shows 'for 3, against 5' (picks dressed as people), and the verdict's '4 answered' against the count line's '6 answered' made me stop and work out which number is which.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Importance and its belief line is word for word the one I checked: getting the broken machine running again fast is one of the two hard things they'd most like made easier.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it doesn't tell me I need just one more counted technician, or that 3 of my 4 already put it in their two.
screens.why_b5: n is visible and the screen says plainly it's a small group, 'a lean, not a call', but every second pick is marked 'against', so the strip shows 5 against when only Bogdan actually put two others first, which overstates the case against me.
screens.instead: 3 of the 4 technicians you could count put getting the machine back up in their two, and only Bogdan put two others first; that leans your way, but you need one more counted answer to call it, so send the study to another technician.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside the deciding number, '4 answered · 5 needed to call it', and the So line repeats the same 4 of 5.
screens.why_b2: The answers counted and the line are plain, but 'your bar · 3 of 4' reads like the bar is 3 of 4 when my bar is 2 in 3 and 3 of 4 is the result, and one ghost cell next to two people not counted takes a second look.
screens.why_b3: The title and the belief line are word for word the Current solution belief I checked, asking whoever has seen the fault or digging through OEM manuals.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it does not tell me that one more counted technician would decide it, or that 3 of 4 already leans my way.
screens.why_b5: 6 answered and 4 counted are both visible, the two not counted are named with the reason, and the small group is called 'a lean, not a call'.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 3 of 4 counted technicians fell short of 'Found it, logged a line or two', which leans your way; one more counted answer decides it, so send the study to another technician who had a breakdown this week.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' is stated with '4 answered · 5 needed to call it' beside it, but the Insights screen only shows Importance -- Current solution, which I also checked and which also stopped at 4, has no box here and no line saying why it is missing.
screens.why_b3: The dimension name and the belief line are word for word the Importance belief I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do next -- not to get more technicians answering, not whether one senior tech naming planned work and thin staffing should change how I pitch to the plant.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible everywhere (4 answered, 1 against, On their own (1)) and nothing is claimed beyond that one voice.
screens.why_b6: Bogdan's quote names planned work slipping and too few technicians as heavier than breakdowns -- the 'one guy' himself seeing it differently -- which I had not typed, but it is one person, so it hints at a theme rather than teaching it.
screens.instead: Too few to call on Importance (4 of 5 needed) and Current solution (4 of 5, no why asked); the one against -- the senior tech everyone calls -- says planned work and short staffing weigh more than breakdowns; get at least one more technician through before reading either line.

screens.why1: It is the first screen and checks I am the right kind of tech before anything else, so it is obvious why it is asked.
screens.why2: I get it on one read, but nobody on the floor says a plant 'runs its own maintenance teams'; we say we have an in-house maintenance department or crew, and it is one crew, not teams.
screens.why3: I know whether my plant keeps its own maintenance department or contracts the work out.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it for a gate question, and a gate carries no escape.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's segment of US plants with their own maintenance and gives away nothing about any product.
screens.why6: It is short and one question, but 'I'll read 2 options. Yes; or No.' is clunky said aloud, when the screener's spoken form should just be the stem then 'Yes or no.'
screens.instead: Do you work at a US plant that has its own in-house maintenance department? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after confirming I work at a plant with our own maintenance crew, asking if a machine went down this week is the obvious next thing before asking me about it.
screens.why2: "A machine on your line went down" is exactly how we talk on the floor, and "last 5 working days" is clear.
screens.why3: I know whether something went down this week, because I'm the one who got called to it.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but the gate carries two escape chips where it should have none, "I'd rather not say" isn't an allowed escape at all, and "I can't recall one particular breakdown" doesn't fit a yes-or-no about whether one happened.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's "machine on the line goes down" and tells me nothing about any product.
screens.why6: One short question ending in "Yes or no" is easy to hear once and answer, and the chips aren't read aloud.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, did a machine you look after go down? (Yes / No, no escape chips)

screens.why1: Right after I said yes, a machine went down this week, asking how many days it happened is the obvious next thing to ask.
screens.why2: Plain shop talk: working days, a machine going down, how many days; I'd answer it on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know which days I got called to a down machine this week, though I cover more than one line, so 'your line' to me means whatever I'm responsible for.
screens.why4: 1 to 5 covers every answer once I've already said yes, none of them overlap, and I can't recall fits as the way out.
screens.why5: It just asks how often machines go down, with nothing about anybody's product or plan slipping through.
screens.why6: Short and one question, and 'a number from 1 to 5' is easy to hold, so I'd hear it once and say a number.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, on how many days did a machine you look after go down? 1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5 · I can't recall

screens.why1: After asking whether and how often a machine went down this week, asking which part of that week I'd most like made easier follows naturally.
screens.why2: Parts, short-handed shifts, PMs and getting a down machine back up are all things I'd say myself, and I get it on first hearing.
screens.why3: I live this every week, so I can pick one straight from last week without guessing.
screens.why4: Two things are missing: figuring out what's actually wrong when nobody's seen the fault before or it's buried in the manual, and writing up the fix afterward. 'Getting the broken machine running again fast' also overlaps with 'getting the right spare parts in time', since waiting on parts is usually why it isn't fast.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks, but the founder's job has two halves, running again fast and leaving a record of the fix, and the record half has dropped out of the list.
screens.why6: It's one short question with five short, parallel options I can hold by ear, and one escape said last.
screens.instead: Think of your last week on the line. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Figuring out what's wrong with the machine · Getting the right spare parts in time · Covering the shift with too few technicians · Keeping up with planned maintenance · Writing up what you fixed -- or None of these

screens.why1: After asking what I'd most like made easier, it makes sense to ask how my last breakdown actually went.
screens.why2: It's two things in one breath, asking somebody or digging through the OEM manuals, and "whoever has seen the fault" isn't how I'd say it; I'd say the guy who's seen it before.
screens.why3: I know exactly how my last breakdown went, who I called, what I looked up and what I wrote in the log.
screens.why4: Each option packs two things together, how I found the fix and how much I logged, so "found it fast, logged nothing" has no home; calling the OEM tech or vendor is missing; and the escape should be about someone else doing it, not recall.
screens.why5: Manuals, the one guy who knew, and logging the fix are my world; I don't see a product being sold to me.
screens.why6: It's short enough to hear, but the stem's either-or and the options carrying two halves each make five of them hard to hold by ear.
screens.instead: Think of your last breakdown. How did you find the fix? Knew it myself; asked the guy who'd seen it before; dug through the OEM manual; called the OEM or vendor tech; or trial and error while the line was down. Or say someone else handled it. Then: What did you write in the log? A proper record of the fix; a line or two; or almost nothing.
